title: Abstraction
content:
Learning is stronger when it matters, when the abstract is made concrete and personal.
As part of using abstraction and elaboration, putting new knowledge into a larger context that you have some experience with helps learning

title: Confidence based on repeated performance
content: There's a difference between feeling confident of your knowledge and demonstrating mastery. When confidence is based on repeated performance, demonstrated through testing that simulates real world conditions, you can lean into it.

title: Consolidation
content: This is the process of strengthening memory traces and storing them into long term memory. Essentially, you're letting the new learning cook as you internalize it and go over it again and again to make sense of it. This is an active process that needs to be fostered and patience needs to be employed here since it takes time for new learning to fully consolidate When practicing something over and over in rapid fire, you're leaning on short term memory and very little mental effort is required. You show self-satisfying results and get a sense of quick improvement (i.e. Illusion of mastery). However, that doesn't do much in terms of solidifying your learning. Your performance in the moment is not and indication of durable learning. It's best to let the memory recede a little and make the effort to retrieve it in order for the learning to be more lasting (i.e. Spaced repetition).

title: Encoding
content: Converting sensory perceptions into mental representations of the observed patterns. There representations are called memory traces much like notes jotted down on a scratchpad or short term memory.

title: LSP
content: My Initial Understanding I understand this as being a server that enriches the code editor with programming language specific functionalities and symbol indexing. What is LSP? Also known as Language Server Protocol This is a JSON-RPC-based communication protocol that is used between IDEs and servers that provide language intelligence tools. These tools include syntax highlighting code completion linting refactoring warning and error detection (similar to getting compilation errors before you compile the code? Unless the LSP compiles on your behalf and generates the errors?) This is pretty open-source and once an LSP for a language is built, it can be used with any IDE that supports the protocol. LSP was developed by Microsoft back in 2016 and is now open source. The spec can be found in the official github repo With LSP, the code editor acts as a client to some LSP server (where is the LSP server hosted?) LSP does not make any provisions about about how requests are transferred between client and server. Client and Server could be in the same process or on different machines. References https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/ - Official overview and specification of the protocol https://github.com/microsoft/language-server-protocol - Implementation of the protocol https://langserver.org/ - for LSP implementations.

title: Learning
content: What Is Learning? Learning is the acquisition of knowledge and skills. All new learning requires a foundation of prior knowledge, so in some way, learning is an iterative process that relies on making connections to existing knowledge and experiences. Learning is better when it is harder, for it yields better mastery of the topic and longer retention compared to when it's made "easy". The book Make It Stick talks in depth about learning and is where most of the concepts in this and related notes originate from. You learn better when you go wide (i.e. BFS), drawing on all of your aptitudes and resourcefulness Learning Building Blocks All forms and practices of learning are built atop one or more of the following concepts, hence them being coined building blocks. Encoding Consolidation Retrieval Practice Generation effect Elaboration Spaced repetition Abstraction These building blocks are incorporated into Learning patterns that reliably lead to long lasting learning. Note that there are Learning anti-patterns that degrade the learning experience and yield subpar results given the time it takes to execute on them. How Learning Occurs The learning process roughly follows these steps: Encoding - the process of converting sensory perceptions into mental representations of observed patterns called memory traces Consolidation - the process of strengthening memory traces and storing them in long term memory Retrieval - the act of remembering memory traces stored in long term memory For learning to be durable, in addition to the step-by-step process described prior, one needs to associate the new material with a diverse set of cues that will help in recalling that knowledge. This is often done in the form of relating to prior knowledge (hence why new learning requires prior knowledge). [!info] This is self-aggrandizing but I was able to do this instinctively when I was younger (was I a savant like that?) Knowledge, skills, and experiences that are vivid and hold significance, and those that are periodically practiced, stay with us. What Does It Take To Learn? Retrieval for the sake of learning Reflection is a form of practice Testing Effect Exploring Nuances The greater the effort to retrieve learning, provided that you succeed, the more that learning is strengthened by retrieval. Giving students corrective feedback after tests keeps them from incorrectly retaining material they have misunderstood and produces better learning of the correct answers Adding Variety TBD Embracing Difficulty When learning is difficult it yields better understanding and remembering. One should embrace the difficulties that come with learning and be patient with how apparently "slow" the learning becomes compared to other methods that seem easy but give you an Illusion of mastery. That learning will yield results in the short term that seem very desirable but in actuality, does not last long. The old adage To go fast, first go slow applies here. Difficulty forces us to slow down and truly internalize what is being learned or trained (e.g. Mia Blundetto's PLF practice). Rather than having an illusion of master, it's best to have Confidence based on repeated performance. And that can be achieved by learning with an embrace for the difficulty that comes with it. However, not all difficulty in learning is the same. There's desirable and undesirable difficulties Desirable Difficulties These are short-term impediments that are favorable for long-term learning. Reconsolidation of Memory During a focused, effortful recall, the learning is made pliable again: the most salient aspects of it become clearer, and the consequent reconsolidation helps to reinforce meaning, strengthen connections to prior knowledge, bolster the cues and retrieval routes for recalling it later, and weaken competing routes. Creation of Mental Models Mental Models are forms of deeply entrenched and highly efficient skills or knowledge structures that, like habits, can be adapted and applied in varied circumstances. And doing these is rather hard but it provides significant benefits in the long run. Variability Retrieval difficulties posed by spacing, interleaving, and variation are overcome by invoking the same mental processes that will be needed when applying the learning to practice. [!quote] Practice like you play, and you'll play like you practice. [!quote] The only thing that won't betray you is your training History's Strongest Disciple Kenichi [!quote] Not everyone who works hard is rewarded. But, all those who succeeded have worked hard Hajime No Ippo Related Notes building a plane while in mid-air Work-life balance feels like a myth if your goal is to get ahead Conceptual Learning

title: MCP
content:
Also know as Model Context Protocol
What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?
Copy page
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems.Using MCP, AI applications like Claude or ChatGPT can connect to data sources (e.g. local files, databases), tools (e.g. search engines, calculators) and workflows (e.g. specialized prompts)—enabling them to access key information and perform tasks.Think of MCP like a USB-C port for AI applications. Just as USB-C provides a standardized way to connect electronic devices, MCP provides a standardized way to connect AI applications to external systems.

[​
](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/getting-started/intro#what-can-mcp-enable%3F)
What can MCP enable?

Agents can access your Google Calendar and Notion, acting as a more personalized AI assistant.
Claude Code can generate an entire web app using a Figma design.
Enterprise chatbots can connect to multiple databases across an organization, empowering users to analyze data using chat.
AI models can create 3D designs on Blender and print them out using a 3D printer.

[​
](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/getting-started/intro#why-does-mcp-matter%3F)
Why does MCP matter?
Depending on where you sit in the ecosystem, MCP can have a range of benefits.

Developers: MCP reduces development time and complexity when building, or integrating with, an AI application or agent.
AI applications or agents: MCP provides access to an ecosystem of data sources, tools and apps which will enhance capabilities and improve the end-user experience.
End-users: MCP results in more capable AI applications or agents which can access your data and take actions on your behalf when necessary.

title: Reflection is a form of practice
content: Reflection can involve several cognitive activities that lead to stronger learning: retrieving knowledge and earlier training from memory (think Retrieval Practice) connecting these to new experiences (think Elaboration) visualizing and mentally rehearsing what you might do differently next time (think Elaboration) (I'm unsure if the context below fits in this note.) You need to memorize the list of things that you need to worry about in a given situation: steps A, B and C; and you will drill on them. (this makes sense for foundational knowledge and well established procedures). Then there comes a time when you get into a tight situation and it's no longer a matter of thinking through the steps, it's a matter of reflexively taking the correct action. Unless you keep recalling this maneuver, it will not become a reflex. (Think about things in your job or your life that you do. The things that need to become a reflex, or second nature, or whatever, need to be drilled as described in the paragraph above) Reflection - the act of taking a few minutes to review what has been learned from an experience and asking yourself questions. Some good reflection questions to ask after learning a new concept (or attending a lecture): what are the key ideas? what are some examples? how do these relate to what I already know? Some good reflection questions to ask after an experience what went well? what could have gone better? what might I need to learn for better mastery? what strategies might I use the next time to get better results? Reflection can involve Retrieval Practice, Elaboration, and Generation effect

title: Retrieval Practice
content: Retrieval practice (the act of recalling facts from memory) strengthens the memory and interrupts forgetting. A single, simple quiz after reading a text or hearing a lecture produces better learning and remembering than rereading the text or reviewing lecture notes. while the brain is not a muscle that gets stronger with exercise, the neural pathways that make up a body of learning do get stronger, when the memory is retrieved and memory is practiced. The Cap on Retrieval There's a lower cap on retrieval than there is on learning. Not every memory you have stored is readily available for you to retrieve. If that were the case, it would be really hard to sort through all your memories when thinking and making decisions. Part of that lower cap on retrieval is that the ability to recall knowledge is determined by the context, recent use, and the number of vivid cues linked to that piece of knowledge. And often times, these cues need to be updated in order to match the current status quo. (e.g. updating cues from a previously learned language to support the learning of a new language). However, when mastery is achieved, it's safe to forget because that knowledge is easily relearned. The knowledge itself is not forgotten, it's the cues that help retrieve it that have been forgotten. Diminishing Returns The easier the knowledge or skill is for you to retrieve, the less your retrieval practice benefits the retention of it. How to practice retrieval Quizzes Flashcards with Spaced repetition Writing down 10 facts you did not know about what you read Retrieval and Elaboration Using AI for self-testing

title: Testing Effect
content: A tool to build mastery of any topic In virtually all areas of learning, you build better mastery when you use testing as a tool to identify gaps and bring forth areas of weakness We lose around 70% of what we've just heard or read. Practicing retrieval makes learning stick far better than re-exposure to the original material does. This is the testing effect, AKA the retrieval-practice effect. Pitting the learning of basic knowledge against the development of creative thinking is a false choice The Testing Effect in the Lab Researchers showed that simply asking a subject to fill in a word's missing letters resulted in better memory of the word. This experience was a demonstration of what researchers call the Generation effect The modest effort required to generate the cued answer while studying the pairs strengthened memory of the target word tested later. This study found that the ability to recall the word pair on later tests was greater if the practice retrieval was delayed by twenty intervening word pairs than when it came immediately after first studying the pair. The Testing Effect in the Wild After reading passages, write down ten facts they hadn't known before reading the passages.

title: All new learning requires a foundation of prior knowledge
content:
Having knowledge is necessary for long term learning for without knowledge, you don't have the foundation for the higher level skills of analysis, synthesis, and creative problem solving.

[!quote] One cannot apply what one knows in a practical manner if one does not know anything to apply.

Mastery requires both the possession of ready knowledge ad the conceptual understanding of how to use it.

Because learning is based on prior knowledge, the more we learn, the more possible connections we create for learning, i.e. the more we learn the more are able to learn.

title: Elaboration
content: Elaboration is the process of giving new material meaning by expressing it in your own words and connecting it with what you already know.

title: Generation effect
content: This is the act of exerting some amount of effort to generate an answer given a cue. Generating an answer can be translated to remembering. If I have breadcrumbs of the information I'm trying to retrieve, I spend more mental effort recalling that information and that leads to better remembering.

title: Illusion of mastery
content:
Increased familiarity with a piece of information and fluency when ingesting it can create the illusion that we have mastery over it.
In the case of a piece of text, the fact that one can repeat the contents from memory doesn't necessarily mean that a solid understanding of the contents has been achieved. That shows no indication that one understands the core principles, their applications and their links to other concepts.

title: Spaced repetition
content: When you space out practice at a task and get a little rusty between sessions, or you interleave the practice of two of more subjects, retrieval is harder and feels less productive, but the effort produces longer lasting learning and enables more versatile application of it in later settings.
